asr_transcript: Early images from the James Webb Space Telescope suggested massive galaxies were unexpectedly common when the universe was young. This paper asks a narrower question. Do observed counts exceed the Elistris-TNG computer simulation by more than plausible errors in estimated stellar mass? Here, abundance means cumulative number density. How many galaxies occupy a given volume above a mass threshold? The threshold is 10 to the power 10.5 solar masses or about 32 billion times the sun's mass. At Redshift 5, an early cosmic era, observations report about three times 10 to the minus five galaxies in each cubic megaparsec, a standard cosmic volume unit. Elistris-TNG reports 1.1 times 10 to the minus five, a raw factor of 2.7. The high mass tail is steep, so small mass changes move many objects across the cutoff. A 0.28-dex downward shift, a logarithmic change equal to dividing masses by about 1.9, erases the Redshift 5 to 6 excess. That adjustment is smaller than the roughly one-deck stellar mass systematic budget summarized for recent studies. One-deck means a factor of 10. Contributors include model fitting choices, assume stellar birth masses, bright galactic nuclei, and measurement scatter that boosts the apparent high mass count. At Redshift 7 to 9, candidates selected from their light show a larger apparent excess, around 13 fold. The calculation requires a 0.44-dex correction or dividing masses by about 2.8. Their masses remain unconfirmed by spectroscopy. Do not extend this conclusion to every early galaxy. Spectroscopically confirmed quiescent galaxies, systems with little star formation, above Redshift 6, remain roughly 2-dex or 100-fold above baseline predictions. The paper says this distinct residual is unresolved by those systematics. At Redshift's 4 to 6, the counts do not require new cosmology once mass uncertainties are allowed.
